claims.text: Configurational entropy is the primary factor governing premelting and melting behavior in HEA nanoparticles.
Configurational entropy suppresses grain-boundary mobility in HEA nanoparticles.
Suppressed grain-boundary mobility stabilizes the solid phase.
Solid-phase stabilization raises the melting point of HEA nanoparticles relative to comparable low-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Changing the number of principal elements from binary to ternary to quinary changes configurational entropy.
Atomic-level disorder and configurational entropy influence grain-boundary structure and mobility.
High configurational entropy disrupts grain-boundary migration.
Disrupted grain-boundary migration reduces the tendency for surface premelting.
Nanoparticles with higher configurational entropy will have a later onset of premelting than comparable low-entropy nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with higher configurational entropy will have higher melting points than comparable low-entropy nanoparticles.
The delay in premelting and increase in melting point scale with the number of principal elements.
Binary low-entropy alloy nanoparticles are expected to premelt earlier and melt at lower temperatures than the HEA nanoparticles.
The proposed relationship should hold for nanoparticles containing at least four principal elements, below 50 nm, and without drastic atomic-radius or bonding-type mismatch.
Surface segregation or local ordering may confound the proposed configurational-entropy effect.

contradictions.description: The comparison is described as involving low-entropy and HEA nanoparticles of similar composition, but the intervention changes the number of principal elements. The particles therefore cannot have the same overall elemental composition, and the intended meaning of 'similar composition' is not defined.
